primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Diffuse hepatic fibrosis and regenerative nodules increase intrahepatic resistance, causing portal hypertension, ascites, varices, and splenomegaly.
vignette: A 58-year-old man with long-term alcohol use has ascites, splenomegaly, esophageal varices, and a nodular liver.
distractor_notes: Acute hepatitis does not typically cause chronic nodular remodeling and varices.
Budd-Chiari can cause portal hypertension but requires hepatic venous outflow obstruction; the chronic diffuse nodular liver and alcohol history support cirrhosis.
Nephrotic syndrome causes edema but not varices and nodular liver.
Pneumonia does not cause portal hypertension.
key_expl: Chronic liver scarring with portal-hypertensive complications is cirrhosis.
objective: Recognize cirrhosis from structural and portal-hypertensive findings.

sources.support: NIDDK describes cirrhosis as chronic liver scarring causing portal hypertension and related complications.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilation reduce effective arterial volume, activating RAAS and sodium retention; low albumin can further favor fluid movement into the peritoneum.
vignette: A patient with decompensated cirrhosis develops tense ascites and secondary hyperaldosteronism.
lead: Which renal response most directly promotes continued fluid accumulation?
distractors: Reduced water reabsorption despite high vasopressin
distractor_notes: Cirrhosis causes avid sodium retention, not natriuresis.
Effective arterial underfilling activates, not suppresses, renin.
Aldosterone rises in decompensated cirrhosis.
Vasopressin-mediated water retention also increases.
key_expl: Reduced effective arterial volume activates RAAS and renal sodium retention, expanding extracellular fluid and ascites.
objective: Explain renal sodium retention in cirrhotic ascites.

sources.support: NIDDK describes portal hypertension, ascites, and sodium-water retention in cirrhosis.

sources.support: MedlinePlus describes fluid accumulation in the abdomen due to cirrhosis and portal hypertension.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of pancreatic lipase and other digestive enzymes impairs nutrient digestion, especially fat, causing steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
vignette: A patient with chronic pancreatitis has bulky greasy stools, weight loss, and low levels of vitamins A, D, E, and K.
lead: Loss of which pancreatic secretion most directly causes the steatorrhea?
distractor_notes: Insulin is endocrine and affects glucose metabolism.
Glucagon is endocrine.
Bicarbonate neutralizes acid but isolated loss is not the main cause of fat maldigestion.
Amylase digests carbohydrate, not fat.
key_expl: Pancreatic lipase is essential for triglyceride digestion; deficiency causes steatorrhea.
objective: Link pancreatic exocrine failure to lipase deficiency and fat malabsorption.

sources.title: Chronic Pancreatitis
sources.support: NIDDK describes pancreatic enzyme deficiency, maldigestion, and steatorrhea in chronic pancreatitis.

sources.title: Pancreatic diseases
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes pancreatic digestive enzyme production and exocrine disease.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Reduced brush-border lactase leaves lactose unabsorbed, causing osmotic diarrhea and bacterial fermentation with bloating and gas.
vignette: A 27-year-old man develops abdominal bloating, flatulence, and watery diarrhea several hours after drinking milk. Symptoms resolve when dairy is avoided.
distractor_notes: Celiac disease causes broader malabsorption and is not limited to lactose exposure.
IBD produces inflammatory symptoms and often blood or systemic findings.
Pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhea rather than isolated dairy-triggered symptoms.
Dysentery is infectious and often bloody.
key_expl: Dairy-triggered bloating and osmotic diarrhea are classic lactase deficiency.
objective: Recognize lactose intolerance from dietary trigger and symptom pattern.

sources.title: Lactose intolerance
sources.support: NIDDK describes lactase deficiency causing gas, bloating, and diarrhea after lactose intake.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Inflammation and microperforation of a colonic diverticulum, usually in the sigmoid colon, causes left lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis.
vignette: A 67-year-old woman has fever and constant left lower quadrant abdominal pain with focal tenderness.
distractor_notes: Appendicitis usually localizes to the right lower quadrant.
Crohn disease is typically chronic and may involve terminal ileum.
Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant or epigastric pain.
IBS does not cause fever and focal inflammatory tenderness.
key_expl: Fever with focal LLQ tenderness in an older adult is classic sigmoid diverticulitis.

sources.title: Diverticulitis

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Colonic bacteria ferment unabsorbed carbohydrates and fiber to short-chain fatty acids, which colonocytes can use as fuel and which influence water and electrolyte absorption.
vignette: Dietary fiber reaches the colon undigested by human enzymes.
lead: What is a major product of bacterial fermentation of this fiber?
distractors: Bile acids synthesized de novo by colonocytes
distractor_notes: Primary bile acids are synthesized by hepatocytes.
Pancreatic lipase is produced by pancreas.
Pepsin is produced in stomach.
Intrinsic factor is produced by gastric parietal cells.
key_expl: Gut bacteria convert fermentable fiber into short-chain fatty acids such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate.
objective: Identify a key metabolic product of colonic bacterial fermentation.

sources.title: Digestive System: How It Works
sources.support: NIDDK describes large-intestinal bacterial processing of undigested material.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Chronic cirrhosis and viral hepatitis increase risk for primary hepatocellular malignancy, which may present with worsening liver disease, mass, weight loss, and elevated alpha-fetoprotein.
vignette: A 59-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B develops weight loss and a new liver mass. Alpha-fetoprotein is markedly elevated.
distractor_notes: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from bile ducts and is not characteristically associated with AFP elevation.
Pancreatic cancer is extrahepatic.
Hepatic adenoma is benign and associated with hormones or anabolic steroids.
Metastatic colon cancer can form liver masses but does not fit the classic HBV-AFP pattern.
key_expl: Chronic HBV with a liver mass and elevated AFP strongly suggests hepatocellular carcinoma.
objective: Recognize HCC risk factors and tumor marker association.
clues: new liver mass with high AFP

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Some gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors produce serotonin; liver metastases can allow vasoactive mediators to reach systemic circulation and cause flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, and right-sided valvular fibrosis.
vignette: A patient with metastatic ileal neuroendocrine tumor has episodic flushing, watery diarrhea, wheezing, and tricuspid valve disease.
lead: Which mediator is most strongly implicated?
distractor_notes: Insulin excess causes hypoglycemia.
Calcitonin is associated with medullary thyroid cancer.
Aldosterone causes hypertension and hypokalemia.
PTH raises calcium.
key_expl: Carcinoid syndrome is driven largely by serotonin and other vasoactive substances from metastatic neuroendocrine tumors.
objective: Connect carcinoid syndrome with serotonin secretion.
